# Homework Report: Reddit Stock Sentiment (3 classes)


## 1. Data overview and cleaning

For the homework, I ran the same tools on a Reddit stock-sentiment dataset instead of 20 Newsgroups. `load_dataset_tool` loaded 847 posts (`load_dataset_1`): 423 neutral (0.0), 315 negative (-1.0), and just 109 positive (1.0). That is much less balanced than the newsgroup data, and the small positive class could matter later. The first five rows (`inspect_data_2`) had no email headers this time, just the posts themselves. What surprised me was the labels. "Seeing lots of red in the ticker" is labeled neutral, but red means prices are falling. "He didn't say thank you" is labeled negative, even though it contains "thank you." So the sentiment here depends on the whole sentence, not on single words, and I suspected this would make the task harder than topic classification. There were no missing texts (`check_missing_3`), but `check_duplicates_tool` found 23 duplicates (`check_duplicates_4`). I asked the agent what they were, and it said the tool only returns row numbers, not the text. After dropping them (`check_duplicates_5`), I had 813 posts left, so 34 rows were removed, not 23. The agent explained that the count only includes the extra copies, while `keep=False` deletes the original too. I think removing every copy is fine here, since repeated posts like these are most likely bots. The newsgroup data had no duplicates at all. For length (`describe_data_6`), the mean is 148 characters, the median 80, the standard deviation 241, and the longest post 2,753. Negative posts have the longest median (96) and neutral posts the shortest (68). Positive posts vary the most (standard deviation 295). The mean is again above the median, so the data is right-skewed like before. The real difference is length: the newsgroup median was 1,235 characters, about 15 times longer. I expected this alone to change most of the results that followed.

## 2. Document-term matrix and variance filtering

I built the document-term matrix with `build_dtm_tool` (`build_dtm_7`), again removing English stop words. It has only 4,072 terms, compared with 35,482 for the newsgroups, which makes sense for fewer and much shorter posts. I asked the agent whether the vocabulary contained anything that was not a real word. It pointed to number strings and explained that CountVectorizer keeps numbers by default. I later noticed didn and ve in the pattern mining results (`mine_patterns_11`). These are pieces of contractions like didn't and I've, cut off at the apostrophe. So both datasets have preprocessing noise, but from different sources: the newsgroups had email headers, domain names, and ID numbers, while Reddit has numbers and broken contractions. The same tool would need different cleaning for each. Before filtering, I had asked the agent how short posts might affect the variance filter. It predicted that most terms would appear only zero or one time per post, giving low variances, so fewer terms would pass the same threshold. That is what happened. With a threshold of 0.01 (`variance_filter_8`), the vocabulary dropped from 4,072 to 340 terms, only 8.3%. The newsgroups kept 14.3% (5,089 of 35,482). Still, I don't think length explains all of it, since the number of posts, the word distribution, and the classes are also different. The top term is trump, with a variance of only about 0.17. The rest of the top 20 includes star, like, market, china, just, graphite, people, money, and company. I see three groups: politics (trump, china, tariffs, republican, president), everyday words (like, just, think), and words that seem to come from a few stock-promotion posts (star, graphite, lithium, aviation). In the newsgroups, jpeg had a variance of about 25, roughly 150 times higher. The Reddit chart also declines slowly, with no single term standing out like jpeg did. My guess is that a short post rarely repeats one word many times, while the very long newsgroup documents could repeat a word dozens of times.

## 3. Pearson vs. Spearman correlation (target: negative)

For the correlation analysis, I used the negative class (-1.0) as the target. In the Pearson result (`pearson_filter_9`), trump ranks first with r ≈ 0.15, followed by words like fuck, china, economy, trade, trust, americans, great, retard, shit, clown, and delusional. They fall into two groups: politics and the economy, and swearing or insults. The one that caught my eye was great. It is normally a positive word, yet here it correlates with negative posts. When I asked the agent why, it suggested two reasons: people may use it sarcastically, or it may appear in phrases like "great depression" or "great loss." I never looked at the posts that contain great, though, so both are guesses, not confirmed causes. The only negative term in the Pearson top 20 is new. The agent thought it might come from posts about new products or news, which tend to be less negative, but that also needs checking against the actual text. I also kept in mind that the target compares 315 negative posts against 498 others, so the class sizes could shape which words rank highest. The Spearman result (`spearman_filter_10`) surprised me because it is almost the same as Pearson. trump is at 0.154, fuck at 0.142, and most of the top terms overlap, with stocks as the main new negative term. On the newsgroups, the two methods disagreed a lot: graphics jumped from 13th place under Pearson to first under Spearman (r ≈ 0.52). I asked the agent why the two are so close this time. It explained that in short posts most words appear zero or one time, so raw counts and ranks are nearly the same thing. In long newsgroup documents, a word can repeat many times, which pulls Pearson but not Spearman. For me, this is the clearest difference between the two datasets: the same two methods agree on short text and disagree on long text. The low correlations also say something. Words like graphics, god, or cancer point to a topic, but sentiment often depends on context, negation, and sarcasm, so a single word rarely tells you how a post feels.

## 4. Frequent pattern mining

For pattern mining, I ran `mine_patterns_tool` with FP-Growth on the negative class, using variance filtering (`mine_patterns_11`). Since the posts are so short, I lowered the minimum support count from 14 (used in the Pipeline) to 5, hoping to find more words that appear together. It found 65 patterns, but every one of them is a single word. There is not a single combination of two or more terms. The words fall into a few groups: negative feelings (worse, worst, lost, delusional, idiot, clown), politics (war, country, allies, congress), and trading or risk (calls, puts, buying, hold, risk). The broken contractions didn and ve also show up, so the preprocessing noise is still there. trump and fuck, which ranked near the top in the correlation analysis, are missing. From what I learned in the Pipeline, I think this is because the tool's variance filter drops the top 5% of terms by variance before mining, but I did not confirm this for these two words. The contrast with the Pipeline is large. With a minimum support of 14, the newsgroups still gave 783 patterns, including combinations like greatly + appreciated. Reddit gave only 65 single words even at 5. I think the main reason is length. A short post contains only a few words, so even when two words are each common, they rarely land in the same post. Long newsgroup documents contain many more words, plus repeated phrases and signatures, so combinations come up much more often. Lowering the threshold for short text was not enough to get patterns like the ones from long text.

## 5. Dimension reduction and conclusion

Finally, I used `reduce_dimensions_tool` to run PCA (`reduce_dimensions_13`) and t-SNE (`reduce_dimensions_14`). PCA keeps only 10.2% of the variance (6.62% and 3.53%), half of the newsgroups' 21.6%. Most posts pile up near the origin, with a few neutral outliers. t-SNE, which partly separated the newsgroup topics, leaves the three sentiments completely mixed. The reason is the task itself. Topics have their own words: god, jpeg, cancer. Sentiment does not. Two posts about the same stock can praise it or attack it with almost the same vocabulary, and "don't trust" is negative because of "don't," not "trust." Single-word counts simply miss this. When I asked the agent whether my tools were general enough, the practical answer was yes: every tool ran on both datasets without changes. But the results were not general. Reddit kept fewer terms (8.3% vs. 14.3%), Pearson and Spearman nearly matched, and FP-Growth found no combinations. A general tool does not give general results. Each dataset has its own problems: the newsgroups suffer from very long documents and email headers, while Reddit suffers from short text, class imbalance, words that rarely appear together, and sentiment that depends on context. To do better on Reddit, I would handle contractions so didn't stays whole, add bigrams to keep phrases like "don't trust," and make `check_duplicates_tool` return the duplicated text so I can decide what to keep. Running the same pipeline twice showed me that a tool running without errors is only the start. I still have to understand the data and question the agent's explanations.
